newsitem.title: USA: Oil writer sees computers cutting into fuel demand.
newsitem.headline: Oil writer sees computers cutting into fuel demand.

text.p: Computer technology and the promise of the Internet are likely to cut into gasoline demand in the coming decades, the author of the oil history, "The Prize," told refining executives.

"The electric car is here and it's not from Detroit. It's coming from Silicon Valley," said Daniel Yergin, president of Boston-based consulting firm Cambridge Energy Research Associates, referring to growing numbers of telecommuters.
"A change is at hand when it comes to personal travel," Yergin told executives attending the annual meeting of the National Petroleum Refiners Association.
"It's telecommuting and the Internet that are competing with Detroit," Yergin said, since people can now go to work or do business online.
"Technology is now providing an alternative to the lifestyle created by the neighborhood gas station," he said.
The aging of the U.S. population will contribute to slowing gasoline demand, since older people tend to drive less.
But he said demand for transportation fuels like diesel and jet fuel would continue to grow more in line with the economy.
"We're going to see a shift toward jet fuel and (diesel) and away from gasoline," he said.

Globally, he said that between now and 2010, 60 percent of overall energy demand growth would come out of Asia, 20 percent out of Latin America with the remaining 20 percent split about evenly between the United States and Europe.
He said the tendency toward jet fuel and diesel demand at the expense of gasoline was also taking place internationally, in part because those areas already favor diesel over gasoline.

For U.S. refiners who have been boosting gasoline output relative to diesel and jet fuel in recent years, the trend Yergin was describing might be the latest twist in a story of overcapacity and poor profitability.
In the face of such challenges that are cutting into profitabilty, Yergin said efforts to cut costs were likely to continue in the form of the consolidations now sweeping the industry.
"Alliances and mergers are the continuation of cost cutting by other means," Yergin said, adding that while alliances may now be popular, their positive effects on the bottom line are finite.
